title: Cross-runtime callpath proposal and runbook for TRT/Triton/Custom integration
content:
Purpose:
This note captures pragmatic design decisions and a lightweight operational runbook for integrating multiple runtime backends (TensorRT, Triton, and our custom CUDA kernels) into a single serving path. It summarizes experiments we ran, tradeoffs, a proposed adapter-based architecture, safety checks, and an actionable rollout plan.

Background / problem statement:
We need a single, maintainable serving surface that allows per-model and per-request routing to:
- TensorRT (TRT) optimized kernels for high-throughput batched workloads
- Triton backend for model management and multi-framework compatibility
- Custom in-house kernels (low-latency, memory-efficient ops) for streaming/chat cases

Challenges observed in previous prototyping:
- Cross-runtime call overhead (cudaMemcpy, context switches, synchronization points) dominates at short sequences.
- KV cache affinity: switching runtimes mid-conversation forces KV materialization and expensive copies, increasing tail latency.
- Memory fragmentation when liberally loading different runtime artifacts on the same GPU over time.
- Kernel warmup and compilation latency (TRT engines) cause cold-start spikes for rarely used model shards.
- Observability fragmentation: different backends emit inconsistent telemetry which makes end-to-end tracing hard.

Goals for the integration: (measurable)
1) P95 token latency for short (<=128) streaming requests should not regress more than 10% vs current best-in-class single-backend path.
2) End-to-end token cost should remain within 5% of current cost baseline for mixed workloads.
3) Fallbacks must preserve correctness of decoding/kv semantics and avoid partial-state corruption.
4) Operator runbook for safe rollback with automated detection of regressions.

Experiment summary (what we ran):
- Microbench #1: single-op latency for attention + ffn kernels across TRT, Triton (TF/ONNX), and our custom CUDA kernels. Measured device-to-device copy overhead when moving KV between allocators.
- Microbench #2: stream decoding latency with prewarmed and cold TRT engines; quantized vs fp16 runs.
- KV affinity probe: run chat sessions with cross-runtime migration (first N tokens on custom kernels, then switch to TRT) and measured P50/P95 regressions and memcpy overheads.
- Memory churn test: repeated load/unload of Triton model instances + TRT engines to measure fragmentation and allocation latency.
- End-to-end throughputs: mixed-ratio workloads (10/30/60 split of short/medium/long sequences) using adaptive batching enabled.

Key experimental takeaways (data-driven):
- Cross-runtime memcpy cost: moving a 6MB KV state between allocator domains costs ~1.8-2.4ms on A100 PCIe (depends on pinned buffer path). For many short requests this dominates tail latency.
- Keeping KV in-place and routing compute to where the KV already lives reduces P95 by up to 35% in chat-case tests.
- TRT gives best throughput for long sequences but has nontrivial engine compile time (200–1500ms depending on sequence/optimization); TRT warm pool amortizes this but increases memory footprint.
- Custom kernels shine for sub-256 tokens with streaming (lower overhead, zero-copy KV access) but are slower for long sequences due to less aggressive operator fusion.
- Triton provides operational niceties (model lifecycle, metrics) but adds an extra process boundary that can add 0.3–0.8ms in the fast path.

Design constraints we must respect:
- No request-level prometheus metrics should be lost when routing across backends.
- State (KV cache, RNG, decoding context) must be single-source-of-truth logically even if physically sharded.
- Rollouts must be reversible without manual intervention.

Proposed architecture (high level):
1) Callpath Adapter (CPA) — a small, in-runtime component that normalizes calls across backends. Responsibilities:
   - Present a single call API to upper layers (Serve handler).
   - Manage per-request kernel affinity hints and migration semantics.
   - Provide E2E tracing spans and standard telemetry tags.
   - Coordinate safe handoff of KV (see below).

2) KV Cache Manager (KVM) — logical KV manager with physical shards pinned to an allocator/runtime. KVM maintains metadata: owner_runtime, eviction policy, last_access_ts. KVM exposes two primitives:
   - directAccess(runtime) — gives zero-copy access when runtime owns the shard.
   - migrate(shard, src, dst) — asynchronous memcpy + handshake with src/dst to prevent concurrent mutation.

3) Runtime Pools and Warm Pools — TRT engines and custom kernel modules are kept in size-limited warm pools. The CPA queries pool health and makes routing decisions.

Routing heuristics (first-cut):
- Sticky-KV routing: route to runtime that owns the KV shard unless predicted additional cost of running there (queue latency) exceeds migration cost.
- Sequence-length aware: if sequence length > L (configurable, default 1024), prefer TRT for throughput; else prefer custom kernels for latency.
- Cold-engine avoider: if TRT engine is cold and request is latency-sensitive, prefer fallback to custom kernels unless the request is long enough to amortize engine compile.
- Load-aware offload: when GPU occupancy > threshold, route best-effort to lower-cost runtime or enqueue based on priority.

KV migration protocol (simplified run-time-safe handshake):
- CPA requests migrate(shard, src->dst). KVM marks shard "pending_migration".
- New requests that arrive and require the shard are queued temporarily (with bounded wait).
- src produces a consistent snapshot (read-only freeze) via allocator fence and issues an async copy into dst pinned staging buffer.
- dst validates checksum and atomically flips owner_runtime. src garbage collects local transient buffers after acknowledgement.
- If migration takes longer than SLO threshold, CPA triggers circuit-breaker to route to cached snapshot read-only fallback (if safe) or returns throttle signal.

Safety & correctness notes:
- All handoffs must preserve token-generation determinism. That means RNG/state and in-flight partial decode buffers must be drained or checkpointed before migration.
- There must be a single authoritative decoder instance for a conversation. If we migrate compute, we prefer migrating KV ownership rather than moving the decoder state.

Observability requirements (must implement before rollout):
- Unified trace id propagation across Triton grpc/process boundary, TRT engine callbacks, and custom kernel launches.
- Per-request timeline events: queued, dispatched, kernel_start, kernel_end, kv_migrate_start, kv_migrate_end, response_stream_start.
- Custom metric: kv_migration_count, kv_migration_ms, owner_runtime_histogram.

Decision matrix (short):
- Option A: Always run custom kernels for short sequences and TRT for long sequences. Pros: simple, predictable. Cons: poor handling when KV is owned by opposite runtime; causes memcpy.
- Option B: Always prefer runtime that owns KV (sticky-KV). Pros: minimizes memcpy. Cons: may route a long sequence to custom kernel and lose throughput.
- Option C: Hybrid (proposed): Sticky-KV with a cost model that compares queue latency vs migration cost and considers sequence length. Pros: balances cost and latency. Cons: implementation complexity.

We recommend Option C with conservative defaults (favor no migration within first N tokens of a conversation).

Runbook: integration steps for alpha rollout (engineers + SRE):
1) Feature-flag CPA behind runtime gate. Start in Canary cluster with 5% traffic.
2) Enable unified tracing; validate end-to-end traces for 1000 sample requests.
3) Turn on sticky-KV routing but disable automatic migration; collect metrics for owner_runtime distribution and cold-engine events for 48h.
4) Enable asynchronous migration for non-critical workloads with a long wait-time budget. Monitor kv_migration_ms and errors.
5) If telemetry shows increased P95 > target, revert migration flag and iterate on cost model thresholds.
6) Once stable at Canary, increase traffic to 25% then 75% with alerting on: 20% regressions in P95, migration failure rate > 0.5%, memory fragmentation > baseline + 10%.

Safety checks & automated guards (to implement before enabling migration on prod):
- Canary canary-e2e test that runs synthetic conversations and asserts deterministic outputs across backends.
- Auto-rollback hook in rollout service that disables CPA on metric breaches.
- Heap/fragmentation monitor that triggers a graceful drain of instances if fragmentation grows too fast.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Precise cost model: how to quickly estimate migration latency vs queuing penalty at runtime. (Action: Marcus to prototype estimator using recent metrics — due 2026-01-10)
- Cold TRT warm pool sizing tradeoffs for multi-tenant nodes. (Action: Talia to run memory/throughput sweep — due 2026-01-20)
- Consistency model during partial migration: can we allow read-only access to frozen KV while migration proceeds? (Engineering decision required)
- Should we expose sticky-KV affinity as a fine-grained policy per-customer or per-model? (Product + Legal constraint review)

Action items (owners + ETA):
- Implement CPA prototype shim and standard trace propagation (owner: Asha) — prototype by 2025-11-30.
- Instrument KV shard metadata + owner_runtime metric (owner: Omar) — 2025-12-10.
- Build migration handshake + async copy util (owner: Marcus) — 2025-12-20.
- Run extended canary tests and produce a perf report (owner: Talia) — 2026-01-15.

Notes to reviewers (quick):
- This is an intentionally pragmatic design: we prefer conservative migration defaults and strong observability over a theoretically optimal but brittle system.
- Expect follow-ups: a lightweight simulator for migration decisions and a small SDK to ease instrumentation for new kernels.

Appendix: quick perf numbers (selected):
- KV copy 6MB pinned: 2.1ms median, 2.4ms 95th on A100-PCIe.
- TRT cold engine compile: 200–1500ms depending on optimization; warm engine launch ~3–8ms.
- Custom kernel attention op: 0.34ms median for 128x128 blast; TRT fused op: 0.21ms median but needs larger batch to amortize.

If you are reviewing: please comment inline with concrete concerns, especially around migration correctness and rollout safety.

-- Asha (for eng-serving-runtime)
